What You Did Last Week

  • Before the critique, look at the shape of your own week.
  • 1. You found three real designs and read them — Discover
  • 2. You drew rough versions of your own — Ideate
  • 3. You picked one and built it properly — Prototype
  • Those are not arbitrary words. They are phases of a method you have been using without being told its name.

What Is Design Thinking?

  • “Design thinking is a human-centered approach to innovation that draws from the designer's toolkit to integrate the needs of people, the possibilities of technology, and the requirements for business success.” Tim Brown, IDEO
  • Start with people, not with the solution
  • Open up, then narrow down: first the problem, then the answer
  • Make early, and test with the people it is for
  • Loop back when a test says so

The Two You Skipped

  • Define — you chose what to make, but never said who it was for or what it had to do.
  • Test — nobody has checked whether your piece reads.
  • That is what the next half hour is for.

The Verb on Every Brief

  • From here on, each homework opens by naming its phase.
  • Discover — look before deciding
  • Empathize — understand who it is for
  • Define — commit to one reading
  • Ideate — generate quantity, defer judgement
  • Prototype — make it real enough to test
  • Test — let evidence beat preference
  • Deliver — finish and hand it over
  • The verb tells you what a good submission looks like that week.

What Is Visual Hierarchy?

  • Visual hierarchy is the deliberate arrangement of differences that communicates:
  • 1. What matters first
  • 2. What supports it
  • 3. What can wait
  • It turns simultaneous elements into a sequence.

Three Levels of Information

  • Primary — the message or action that must win
  • Secondary — context that supports the primary level
  • Supporting — detail available when needed
  • Every level needs a visible relationship to the others.

Signal and Noise

  • Signal helps the viewer find meaning or act.
  • Noise competes without helping the task.
  • Decoration becomes noise when it claims more attention than its role deserves.
  • Removing noise can strengthen hierarchy without enlarging anything.

Five Attention Drivers

Scale Creates Dominance

  • One clearly larger form becomes the focal point.
  • Equal sizes produce equal claims.
  • The difference—not the absolute measurement—creates hierarchy.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
30 / 83
Scale is relative. If everything is large, nothing is large.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
31 / 83

Weight Can Balance Size

  • A small dense form may balance a larger light form.
  • Ask whether the page feels stable, pulled to one side, or intentionally tense.
  • Balance and hierarchy are related—but not identical.

Channels of Contrast

  • Light versus dark
  • Large versus small
  • Thick versus thin
  • Filled versus outlined
  • Static versus moving
  • Regular versus exceptional
  • ...and many more
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
33 / 83

Violator / Burst Callout

  • A violator deliberately breaks the visual system to announce a genuine exception.
  • Use an unusual contour, angle, overlap, and strong contrast.
  • State one specific claim.
  • Reserve it for information that deserves interruption.
  • Never repeat bursts until they become background noise.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
34 / 83

Position

  • Position influences visibility through:
  • Placement near an expected entry point
  • Isolation from competing elements
  • Proximity to the content it controls
  • Placement at the end of a visual route
  • Position gains meaning from context.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
35 / 83

Entry Points Are Not Universal

  • Reading direction, language, device, task, and learned conventions affect where people begin.
  • Do not treat top-left as a biological law.
  • Support the audience's reading system.
  • Test the real composition in context.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
36 / 83

Space Acts as a Boundary

  • Whitespace does not need a border to separate groups.
  • A spacing system should make group changes visible at a glance.
  • Measure relationships—not isolated gaps.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
37 / 83

Alignment Creates a Route

  • Misaligned elements create several competing entry points.
  • A shared edge gives the eye a dependable route.
  • Break the axis only when the break should be noticed.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
38 / 83

When Drivers Conflict

  • A huge pale heading competes with a tiny saturated button.
  • Ask:
  • Which element wins first?
  • Is that the intended priority?
  • Which cue should be reduced?
  • Which cue should reinforce the winner?

Build a Type Scale by Role

  • Start with roles—not arbitrary point sizes.
  • Display or hero
  • Heading
  • Subheading
  • Body
  • Label or metadata
  • Assign each role a repeatable treatment.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
47 / 83

Size and Weight Form a Matrix

  • Size and weight can reinforce or compensate for each other.
  • Large + bold = maximum emphasis
  • Large + light = spacious emphasis
  • Small + bold = compact signal
  • Small + regular = supporting detail
  • Use the strongest combination sparingly.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
48 / 83

Line Length Shapes Priority

  • A text block is also a visual shape.
  • Long lines feel broad and continuous.
  • Short lines feel compact and emphatic.
  • Very long lines make return paths harder.
  • Different measures can separate roles without changing typeface.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
49 / 83

Leading Creates Texture

  • Line spacing controls density and grouping.
  • Too tight: lines compete and merge.
  • Too loose: the paragraph fragments.
  • Larger display type often needs proportionally tighter leading.
  • Body text needs a stable reading rhythm.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
50 / 83

Labels and Metadata

  • Supporting information should remain accessible without claiming the focal point.
  • Use:
  • Smaller scale
  • Consistent placement
  • Reduced but sufficient contrast
  • Clear proximity to the item described

The Z-Shaped Route

  • A sparse promotional layout can connect four anchors through a broad diagonal route.
  • Useful when:
  • Content density is low
  • The entry and action are clear
  • The route does not fight reading direction

Scanning Depends on the Task

  • People scan differently when they:
  • Search for a known fact
  • Compare products
  • Read a narrative
  • Complete a form
  • Monitor changing data
  • Choose structure from content and user intent—not a fashionable pattern.

Begin with a Content Inventory

  • List every required item before styling.
  • For each item, record:
  • Purpose
  • Audience need
  • Required prominence
  • Relationship to other items
  • Action or decision it supports

Define the Person and Goal

  • Write two sentences:
  • Person: relevant situation, knowledge, and constraint
  • Goal: what they need to understand or accomplish
  • A hierarchy cannot be evaluated without knowing whose task it serves.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
61 / 83

Give One Action the Lead

  • A page may support several actions, but one should normally lead.
  • Primary action: strongest treatment
  • Secondary action: visible alternative
  • Tertiary action: available without competition
  • Equal buttons communicate equal priority.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
62 / 83

The Three-Second Test

  • Show the layout briefly, then hide it.
  • Ask the viewer:
  • 1. What was this about?
  • 2. What seemed most important?
  • 3. What action could you take?
  • Record the answers before explaining.

Studio — One Message, Ten Hierarchies

Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
70 / 83

The Brief

  • Design ten compositions for the same event information:
  • Friday · 19:30
  • The Signals
  • River Hall
  • Doors 18:30 · €12 / €8
  • Tickets
  • Each composition must create a deliberately different reading order.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
71 / 83

Ten Controlled Variations

  • Keep one canvas size and identical wording.
  • Produce ten rapid thumbnails on paper or digitally with a stylus.
  • Develop all ten in the chosen layout application.
  • Let one driver dominate each early variation.
  • Combine drivers deliberately in later variations.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2

Studio Clock (40 min)

Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
73 / 83

Production Workflow

  • 1. Inventory and rank the information.
  • 2. Create one reusable base frame or page.
  • 3. Duplicate it ten times.
  • 4. Change scale, weight, spacing, alignment, contrast, and position.
  • 5. Select the strongest direction and refine it.
  • 6. Export all ten plus the final composition as PDF.
Design & Gestalt · Week 2
Prof. Seb Hirsch · Smart Interactive Media
74 / 83

Peer Test and Critique

  • Show the refined composition for three seconds.
  • Evaluate:
  • Order — what was seen first, second, and third?
  • Clarity — was the event understood?
  • Action — was Tickets discoverable?
  • System — do spacing and alignment feel intentional?
  • Evidence — what changed after the test?

Homework — Hierarchy Variants

  • Define — one message, three reading orders.
  • 1. The message: Campus Christmas Party, a day and a place of your choice in the week of 14 December, free entry.
  • 2. Build three versions, each leading with a different fact: the date, the place, or free entry.
  • 3. Type only, no decoration: scale, weight, contrast, spacing and alignment do the work.
  • 4. One line per version naming the reading order it produces.
  • 5. Keep your sketches and discarded drafts.
